figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Comparative analysis of floral volatiles and genomes of R. banksiae yellow and R. banksiae white
(A) Phenotypes and karyotypes of R. banksiae yellow (RbY) and R. banksiae white (RbW).
(B) Chromatogram of eugenol and coniferyl alcohol in RbW and RbY flowers. WS1, flowers at the first stage of development in RbW. YS1, flowers at the first stage 
of development in RbY. The division of the period of floral development was shown in Figure S1A.
(C) Overview of genomic features along with RbY and RbW. The outer layer represents the genomic landscape of the RbY chromosome (left) and RbW chro-
mosome (right) (a). The other displayed tracks include gene density (b), TE abundance (c), and SV (d), and the relationship between syntenic blocks is indicated by 
connecting lines (e).
(D) Phylogenetic tree of the RbY and RbW species. The numbers on the branches indicate the counts of gene family expansion and contraction. The various 
colored backgrounds of the phylogenetic trees represent distinct branching groups. Gray represents the outgroups that lie beyond the Rosaceae subfamily. 
Green indicates the Amygdaloideae subfamily (outgroups located within the Rosaceae subfamily but outside the Rosoideae). Cyan indicates the outgroups 
located within the Rosoideae subfamily but outside the genus Rosa. Blue represents species closely related to R. banksiae within the genus Rosa.
See also Figures S1 and S2 and Table S1.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Origin and fixation of the SCREP gene in Rosa genus species
(A) SV in the region containing RbSCREP between RbY and RbW. The green link denotes collinear genomic region. The orange link represents the genomic 
position of the RbSCREP gene in RbY and its counterpart in RbW. The gene is highlighted in gray, with the line denoting the intron and the box representing the 
exons.
(B) Genome re-sequencing data indicate that the yellow accessions of R. bankiae have a complete RbSCREP gene, whereas the white accessions have only 
exon 2.
(C) Origin and fixation of the SCREP genes are illustrated through phylogenomics. Phylogenetic tree and divergence time of species (left), distribution of 
RbSCREP and its highly similar sequences in these genomes among various species, and the region collinearity where RbSCREP is located (right). J, Jurassic;

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Functional characterization of key genes related to eugenol biosynthesis in R. banksiae
(A) Correlation analysis of the metabolites in the eugenol biosynthesis pathway with the WGCNA module. The content of caffeic acid, ferulic acid, coniferyl 
aldehyde, and coniferyl alcohol is displayed in Figure S1. These squares represent the correlation between WGCNA modules. The size and color of each square 
indicate the strength of these correlations. The lines illustrate the relationships between modules and metabolites, with different line colors denoting significant 
correlations (p ≤ 0.05).
(B) Correlation of eugenol biosynthesis pathway genes with RbSCREP and eugenol. The circles located on the periphery represent genes associated with the 
eugenol pathway. The color and thickness of the lines represent, respectively, the strength and significance of the correlation between these genes and eugenol 
or RbSCREP. The genes highlighted in red exhibit strong correlation with elevated expression levels.
(C) Schematic of the metabolic pathway from caffeic acid to eugenol.
(D–F) Chromatograms showing the formed products from in vitro assays of RbCOMT1, RbCCR1, and RbREF1 enzymes, respectively. EV, empty vector. Std, 
standard.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Analysis of transcriptional activity of RbSCREP
(A) Expression analysis of RbSCREP in RbW and RbY by both RT-PCR and qRT-PCR.
(B) Subcellular localization of RbSCREP in N. benthamiana and Rosa chinensis.
(C) Schematic of the constructed vectors containing various fragments (P1\P2\P3\P4) for driving the LUC reporter gene. The MITE regions are highlighted in red.
(D) Luciferase (LUC) activity assays were conducted to test the various fragments from the RbSCREP promoter in N. benthamiana.
(E) Activity of RbSCREP promoters of varying lengths.
Different lowercase letters above bars indicate significant differences, as determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test.
See also Data S1.18 and S1.19.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Newly originated taxon-restricted RbSCREP genes serve as a negative regulator in the eugenol biosynthesis pathway
(A) Phenotypes of WT and rose plants overexpressing RbSCREP.
(B) Expression analysis of RbSCREP in rose leaves overexpressing RbSCREP.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Natural alleles of RbSCREP maintain the conserved function
(A) Expression analysis of FaCOMT by qRT-PCR in strawberry fruits overexpressing RbSCREP, RcSCREP, RrSCREP, and RwSCREP, respectively. The control 
group consisted of strawberry fruits transformed with an empty vector (EV).
(B) Eugenol content in strawberry fruit overexpressing RbSCREP, RcSCREP, RrSCREP, and RwSCREP.
(C) Schematic diagrams depicting the effectors and reporters utilized for conducting LUC activity assays in N. benthamiana. pRrCOMT1pro-LUC with EV or 35S-
RrSCREP effector, pRwCOMT1pro-LUC with EV or 35S-RwSCREP effector, and pRcCOMT1pro-LUC with EV or 35S-RcSCREP effector were co-transformed 
into N. benthamiana leaves.
(D) DNA structure and DNA-re-sequencing tracks of the SCREP genes visualized using the IGV browser are presented alongside the numbers of 38 rose species 
or cultivars. The species that contain eugenol in their floral scents are indicated by solid purple circles. The numbers within the circles represent the eugenol 
content (μg/g).
Data represent the mean ± SD (n = 3). Significant differences compared with the EV were determined by the unpaired Student’s t tests: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01. 
See also Figure S7, Data S1.24–S1.25, and Table S4I.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 7. Diversification of rose scent through evolution of a newly originated taxon-restricted gene
Firstly, the emergence of the second exon precedes the formation of the first exon and intron of SCREP during gene birth. Finally, the recruitment of MITE in the 
SCREP promoter significantly enhances the expression of SCREP. SCREP represses the biosynthesis of eugenol. The red dots indicate the presence of eugenol. 
The yellow block represents the second exon of SCREP, while the red and green blocks denote the first exon and intron of SCREP, respectively. The blue block 
illustrates the MITE transposon. The used species are as follows: Arabidopsis thaliana (Ath), Vitis vinifera (Vvi), Malus prunifolia (Mpr), Rubus occidentalis (Roc), 
Fragaria vesca (Fve), Rosa persica (Rpe), Rosa spinosissima (Rsp), Rosa chinensis (Rch), Rosa wichuraiana (Rwi), Rosa banksiae yellow (RbY), Rosa rugosa (Rru), 
and Rosa banksiae white (RbW).
